etymology: Hebrew Obed-Edom, “servant of Edom,” a Levite of Gath in whose house the ark was blessed.
biblical_def: Obed-edom the Gittite was the man in whose house the ark of the LORD rested three months, after Uzzah had been struck down for touching it and David feared to bring it further. “The ark of the LORD continued in the house of Obededom the Gittite three months: and the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household” (2Sa 6:11). When it was told David that the LORD had blessed the house of Obed-edom because of the ark, the king took courage and brought up the ark to the city with gladness (2Sa 6:12). Far from being harmed by the holy thing that had slain Uzzah, Obed-edom and all his house were enriched by it, for he received it with reverence and faith. He was a Levite, and afterward he and his sons were appointed doorkeepers and singers for the ark in its tent, “for God blessed him” (1Ch 26:5); he had eight sons, and his house was multiplied. Obed-edom stands as a beautiful witness that the presence of God, which is death to the irreverent, is blessing and life to those who receive it in faith and fear. The same ark that smote Uzzah enriched Obed-edom; the difference lay not in the ark but in the heart.
webster_summary: A Levite of Gath in whose house the ark rested three months; the LORD blessed him and all his household.
webster_full: OBED-EDOM, a Levite of Gath, a keeper of the ark of the LORD.

His blessing emboldened David to bring up the ark with joy (2Sa 6:12).
He and his sons became doorkeepers and singers for the ark (1Ch 26:5).

Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peulthai the eighth: for God blessed him.

And Shebaniah, and Jehoshaphat, and Nethaneel, and Amasai, and Zechariah, and Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, did blow with the trumpets before the ark of God: and Obededom and Jehiah were doorkeepers for the ark.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses that God’s presence is blessing to the reverent and death to the irreverent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same ark which struck down Uzzah enriched Obed-edom; the difference lay not in the holy thing but in the heart that received it. The presence of God is death to the irreverent and blessing to those who receive it in faith and fear. Men who handle holy things carelessly are warned by Uzzah; those who welcome the presence of God with reverence are blessed like Obed-edom.

Obed-edom’s blessing also rebukes the dread of holiness that has no faith. David at first feared the ark and would not bring it on; but seeing the blessing on Obed-edom’s house, he took courage. The holiness of God is fearful, yet to the believing it is the very fountain of blessing. The reverent soul does not flee the presence of God but draws near in faith, and finds his house enriched.

etymology: Hebrew Kenanyahu, “the LORD establishes” or “whom the LORD sets up,” the chief Levite for song.
biblical_def: Chenaniah was a chief of the Levites in the days of David, set over the song when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem: “Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful” (1Ch 15:22). He was the master of the song, who led the singers in the great procession, “Chenaniah the master of the song with the singers” (1Ch 15:27). His office was to teach and order the music of the house of God, that the praise of the LORD might be offered with skill and reverence by trained voices, not in disorder but in beauty and fitness. The Scripture marks that he was appointed to this work because he was skilful; his gift was recognized and set to its proper use in the worship of God. Chenaniah stands as a witness to the place of trained and skilful music in the worship of the LORD, in the line that leads to the great companies of singers Solomon would establish in the temple. He teaches that the praise of God is to be offered with care and excellence; the LORD is worthy of our best, and the gifts He gives are to be cultivated and devoted to His service in the assembly of His people.
webster_summary: A chief Levite set over the song when the ark came to Jerusalem, the skilful master of the music.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses the place of skilful, reverent music in the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care and excellence due to the praise of God. Chenaniah was set over the song because he was skilful, and he instructed the singers that the worship of the LORD might be offered with beauty and fitness. The praise of God is not to be offered carelessly; the LORD is worthy of our best, and the gifts of music He gives are to be cultivated and devoted to His service.

Chenaniah’s ordered song also stands against both the irreverence that despises beauty in worship and the showmanship that makes worship a performance for men. The aim was the praise of God, offered with skill and reverence by trained Levites under appointed order. True worship is neither slovenly nor self-displaying, but devotes the best of the soul’s gifts to the glory of God in the appointed way.
roots_summary: The name means “the LORD establishes,” from Yah (the LORD) and a verb to set up or establish.

etymology: Hebrew Achyo, “brotherly” or “his brother,” a son of Abinadab who drove the cart bearing the ark.
biblical_def: Ahio was a son of Abinadab, the brother of Uzzah, who together drove the new cart on which the ark of God was carried up from his father’s house in Gibeah toward Jerusalem (2Sa 6:3). “Ahio went before the ark” while Uzzah walked beside it (2Sa 6:4). But the journey ended in sorrow, for the oxen stumbled at the threshingfloor of Nachon, and Uzzah put forth his hand to steady the ark, and the LORD smote him that he died, because the ark had been carried in a way the LORD had not commanded. The ark was meant to be borne upon the shoulders of the Levites by its staves, not drawn upon a cart after the manner of the Philistines; and the careless handling of the holy thing, however well-intended, brought death. Ahio, who went before the ark, is a quiet figure in this solemn scene. His brief appearance is bound up with the great lesson of Uzzah’s death: that God must be approached and served in the way He has appointed, not after the inventions of men. Ahio witnesses, with his brother, that good intentions do not excuse disobedience in the worship of God, and that the holy must be handled with holy fear.
webster_summary: A son of Abinadab who, with his brother Uzzah, drove the cart bearing the ark; he went before it.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his scene teaches that God must be served in the way He appoints.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lesson of the cart and the threshingfloor: the ark was to be borne upon the shoulders of the Levites by its staves, as God commanded, not drawn upon a new cart after the manner of the Philistines. Ahio and Uzzah meant well, but they served God in a way He had not appointed, and Uzzah died. Good intentions do not sanctify disobedience; the LORD is to be worshipped after His own due order, not the inventions of men.

This solemn scene is one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the regulative principle of worship: that what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not to be added by human will. David himself later confessed, “we sought him not after the due order” (1Ch 15:13). The worship of God is His to define; reverent obedience, not creative innovation, is what He requires of His people.

etymology: Hebrew Avinadav, “my father is noble” or “father of willingness,” the man of Kirjath-jearim who kept the ark; not the son of Jesse or of Saul.
biblical_def: Abinadab was a man of Kirjath-jearim in whose house the ark of the LORD abode for twenty years, after it was brought up from Beth-shemesh. When the men of Kirjath-jearim fetched the ark, they brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep it (1Sa 7:1). There the ark rested through the days of Samuel and the early reign of Saul, until David sought it out to bring it up to Jerusalem. Then it was carried from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, driven by his sons Uzzah and Ahio (2Sa 6:3–4). Thus the house of Abinadab was for a generation the resting-place of the throne of God among His people, a quiet hill-house that held the holiest thing in Israel. He is to be distinguished from Abinadab the son of Jesse, David’s brother, and from Abinadab the son of Saul who fell at Gilboa. This Abinadab of Kirjath-jearim is remembered for the long, faithful keeping of the ark in his house, and for the solemn end of that keeping when it was carried away in a manner the LORD had not commanded. His name, “father of willingness,” befits a man who received the ark of God into his home.
webster_summary: The man of Kirjath-jearim in whose house the ark of the LORD rested twenty years; father of Uzzah and Ahio.
webster_full: ABINADAB, a man of Kirjath-jearim who kept the ark of the LORD.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his house witnesses the long keeping of God’s presence and the cost of careless handling.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour and the solemnity of keeping the ark of God. For twenty years the house of Abinadab held the throne of God among His people, while Israel lamented after the LORD. To house the holy things of God is a high privilege, but it is also a weighty charge; the keeping of the ark ended in death when it was at last carried away after the manner of the Philistines rather than as God commanded.

Abinadab’s long keeping of the ark, set beside Israel’s neglect of it during those years, also reminds the reader that the presence of God may be near and yet little sought. The ark abode in the hill-house while the nation drifted; only when Israel lamented after the LORD did the season of recovery begin. Nearness to holy things is no substitute for a heart that seeks the living God.

etymology: Hebrew Tseruyah, perhaps “balm” or “wounded,” the sister of David and mother of his fiercest captains.
biblical_def: Zeruiah was a sister of David, the mother of three of the mightiest and fiercest men of his army: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, the sons of Zeruiah (1Ch 2:16; 2Sa 2:18). Though a woman of whom little personal history is told, her name is woven through the books of Samuel, for her sons are again and again called “the sons of Zeruiah,” men of valour but also of vengeance, whose strong wills more than once troubled the king. Joab was David’s captain, mighty in war but bloody in his vengeance; Abishai was bold and devoted but quick to slay; Asahel was swift of foot and fell young in the pursuit of Abner. David said in his weakness, “these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me: the LORD shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness” (2Sa 3:39). Zeruiah is remembered through her sons, a mother whose offspring were valiant servants of David and yet a grief to him by their hardness. Her name witnesses the weight of a mother’s line in the history of a kingdom, and the mingled blessing and trial of strong and fierce children, whose courage served the throne even as their vengeance vexed it.
webster_summary: A sister of David and mother of his fierce captains Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she witnesses the weight of a mother’s line and the trial of fierce children.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mingled blessing and trial of strong children. Zeruiah’s sons were valiant servants of David, mighty in war, yet their hardness and vengeance grieved the king, so that he confessed they were too hard for him. Courage is a gift, but courage ungoverned by the fear of God becomes cruelty; the strong-willed must be ruled by grace, or their strength turns to a snare.

Zeruiah, remembered only through her sons, also witnesses the quiet weight of a mother’s line in the history of a people. Her name is named again and again, not for her own deeds, but for the men she bore. The Scripture honours the place of mothers in the unfolding of God’s purposes; the sons who shaped a kingdom were the sons of Zeruiah, and her line is not forgotten.

etymology: Hebrew Nachash, “a serpent,” the name of the Ammonite king who besieged Jabesh-gilead.
biblical_def: Nahash the Ammonite was the king who came up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead in the early days of Saul, and his cruelty became the occasion of Saul’s first great victory. When the men of Jabesh sought to make a covenant of peace, Nahash answered that he would make a covenant only on the condition that he might thrust out all their right eyes, to lay it for a reproach upon all Israel (1Sa 11:1–2). When the tidings came to Gibeah, the Spirit of God came upon Saul, and he gathered Israel and delivered Jabesh, smiting the Ammonites until they were scattered (1Sa 11:11). Nahash, “the serpent” by his very name, sought to bring shame and bondage upon the people of God. Yet there was also kindness in him toward David at some earlier season, for David later said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me” (2Sa 10:2). Nahash is remembered chiefly as the cruel oppressor whose insolence stirred up Saul to deliver Israel, a king whose serpent-name fits his proud demand to disgrace the LORD’s people, and whose overthrow displayed the power of God working through His newly anointed king.
webster_summary: An Ammonite king who besieged Jabesh-gilead and demanded the right eyes of its men; defeated by Saul.

And Nahash the Ammonite answered them, On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may thrust out all your right eyes, and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel.

And it was so on the morrow, that Saul put the people in three companies; and they came into the midst of the host in the morning watch, and slew the Ammonites until the heat of the day: and it came to pass, that they which remained were scattered, so that two of them were not left together.
Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants for his father.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his cruelty became the occasion of God’s deliverance through Saul.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the proud cruelty of the oppressor and the deliverance God works against him. Nahash, “the serpent,” sought to bring shame and bondage upon Israel, demanding the right eyes of Jabesh as a reproach. But his insolence stirred up Saul, on whom the Spirit of God came, and Israel was delivered. The LORD often uses the very pride of the wicked to display His power in saving His people.

Nahash’s serpent-name fits the spirit of his demand, for he sought to disgrace and maim the people of God. Yet even this oppressor showed some kindness to David in an earlier day, a reminder that no man is wholly one thing, and that the LORD takes account of every kindness and every cruelty. The serpent who reproached Israel was scattered before the anointed king.

etymology: Hebrew Chanun, “favoured” or “gracious,” the Ammonite king who insulted David’s messengers.
biblical_def: Hanun was the son of Nahash and king of the Ammonites after him, who repaid David’s kindness with a grievous insult that brought war upon his people. When Nahash died, David sought to show kindness to Hanun for his father’s sake, and sent his servants to comfort him (2Sa 10:2). But the princes of Ammon persuaded Hanun that the messengers were spies; so Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their hinder parts, and sent them away in shame (2Sa 10:4). This deliberate disgrace of an embassy of peace was an act of war, and the Ammonites, knowing they had made themselves odious to David, hired the Syrians to fight for them. But the LORD gave Israel the victory over both Ammon and Syria (2Sa 10:6–19). Hanun, whose name means “gracious,” acted with the opposite of grace, turning kindness into an occasion of contempt. He stands as a warning against the folly of repaying goodwill with insult, and the listening to evil counsel that turns a friend into an enemy. His insolence brought ruin upon his own house and people.
webster_summary: The Ammonite king, son of Nahash, who insulted David’s messengers and brought war upon his people.

scriptures: Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants for his father. And David's servants came into the land of the children of Ammon.
Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away.

And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Bethrehob, and the Syrians of Zoba, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men.

Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he warns against repaying kindness with insult and heeding evil counsel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the folly of repaying goodwill with contempt. David sent kindness, and Hanun, listening to suspicious counsellors, returned a deliberate insult that turned a friend into an enemy and brought war upon his land. He that returns evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house (Prov 17:13). The bitter fruit of Hanun’s insolence was the ruin of his people.

Hanun’s heeding of evil counsel is a further warning. His princes filled his ears with suspicion against an embassy of peace, and he believed them to his destruction. Whom a man listens to shapes what he becomes; the counsel of the malicious leads to ruin. His name, “gracious,” stands in sharp rebuke over his graceless act, a reminder that a fair name is no guarantee of a fair heart.

etymology: Hebrew Sheba, perhaps “an oath” or “seven,” a Benjamite rebel against David.
biblical_def: Sheba the son of Bichri was a man of Belial of the tribe of Benjamin, who raised a rebellion against David in the troubled days after Absalom’s revolt. He blew a trumpet and cried, “We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel” (2Sa 20:1), and the men of Israel went up from after David to follow Sheba, though Judah clave to the king. David sent Amasa, then Abishai and Joab, to pursue him; and Joab, having treacherously slain Amasa on the way, chased Sheba to the city of Abel of Beth-maachah and besieged it (2Sa 20:14–15). Then a wise woman of the city cried out to Joab, and learning that he sought only Sheba, she counselled the people in her wisdom; they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and cast it over the wall to Joab, who then blew the trumpet and withdrew (2Sa 20:22). So the rebellion ended with the rebel’s head. Sheba stands as a type of the seditious spirit that despises the LORD’s anointed and sows division among the people of God; his cry of “no part in David” was the very voice of rebellion, and it brought him to a swift and shameful end.
webster_summary: A Benjamite who rebelled against David, crying “We have no part in David”; beheaded at Abel of Beth-maachah.

scriptures: And there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite: and he blew a trumpet, and said, We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel.
So every man of Israel went up from after David, and followed Sheba the son of Bichri: but the men of Judah clave unto their king, from Jordan even to Jerusalem.

The matter is not so: but a man of mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, hath lifted up his hand against the king, even against David: deliver him only, and I will depart from the city. And the woman said unto Joab, Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee over the wall.

Then the woman went unto all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and cast it out to Joab. And he blew a trumpet, and they retired from the city, every man to his tent. And Joab returned to Jerusalem unto the king.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he is a type of the seditious spirit that despises the LORD’s anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ruinous end of the seditious spirit. Sheba’s cry, “We have no part in David,” was the very voice of rebellion against the LORD’s anointed, and it sowed division among the people of God. Those who lift up their hand against God’s appointed order and stir up strife bring destruction upon themselves; Sheba’s rebellion ended with his own head cast over the wall.

The wise woman of Abel offers the brighter contrast. Where Sheba sowed strife, she sought peace, counselling the city to give up the one rebel rather than perish for his sake. Her wisdom saved a city. The Scripture honours the peacemaker who quiets sedition and spares the innocent, even as it shows the certain ruin of the man who sets himself against the throne of David, the type of Christ the King.

etymology: Hebrew Benayahu, “the LORD hath built,” a mighty man of David and captain of his guard.
biblical_def: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was one of David’s mightiest men, a valiant warrior of Kabzeel who did many notable acts: he slew two lionlike men of Moab, he went down and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow, and he slew a goodly Egyptian with the Egyptian’s own spear, which he plucked from his hand (2Sa 23:20–21). For his valour David set him over his bodyguard, the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and he was honoured above the thirty, though he attained not to the first three (2Sa 23:23). Benaiah was steadfastly loyal to David and to Solomon his appointed heir; when Adonijah sought the throne, Benaiah stood with Solomon, and at the king’s command he executed judgment upon Joab, Adonijah, and Shimei, and was set over the host of Israel in Joab’s place (1Ki 2:35). His name, “the LORD hath built,” befits a man whose strength and faithfulness helped establish the throne of David’s house. Benaiah is to be distinguished from Benaiah the Pirathonite, another of the mighty men. He stands as a model of valour joined to loyalty, a strong man whose might was wholly devoted to the LORD’s anointed and the establishing of his kingdom.
webster_summary: A mighty man of David, captain of his guard, loyal to Solomon; slew a lion in a pit in time of snow.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he is a model of valour joined to loyalty in the LORD’s service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is valour joined to faithfulness. Benaiah was a man of great courage, slaying lion and warrior, yet his might was wholly devoted to the LORD’s anointed; he stood with David and then with Solomon, and helped establish the throne. Strength is a gift, but it is honoured only when it serves rightly; Benaiah’s valour was loyal, and so it built up the kingdom rather than troubling it.

Benaiah’s steadfastness when Adonijah sought the throne also commends the loyalty that cleaves to God’s appointed king rather than to the rising faction. When others wavered, Benaiah stood with Solomon, whom the LORD and David had chosen. His name, “the LORD hath built,” was fulfilled in his service, for the faithful strong man is an instrument by which God builds and establishes His kingdom among men.

etymology: Hebrew Zavud, “bestowed” or “given,” the son of Nathan, principal officer and king’s friend under Solomon.
biblical_def: Zabud was the son of Nathan, named among the princes of Solomon as “principal officer, and the king’s friend” (1Ki 4:5). The title “the king’s friend” marks an office of peculiar honour and intimacy, a trusted counsellor and companion near the person of the king, such as Hushai had been to David. Zabud held this place of confidence in the court of Solomon in the days of the kingdom’s greatest glory, when wisdom and wealth and order filled the land. His father Nathan was likely the prophet who had named Solomon and counselled David, or his brother Azariah was over the officers; thus Zabud stood in a family near the very heart of the throne. Little is told of his deeds, but the title he bore speaks of great trust: to be the king’s friend was to be admitted to his counsel and his confidence above the common officers. Zabud’s name, “bestowed” or “given,” befits a man given a place of honour by the king. He witnesses the value of a faithful friend and counsellor near those who bear rule, and the honour of the trusted companion who serves not for gain but in true friendship to the king.
webster_summary: The son of Nathan, principal officer and “the king’s friend” in the court of Solomon.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses the value of a faithful friend and counsellor near those who rule.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of a faithful friend near the seat of rule. Zabud was “the king’s friend,” admitted to Solomon’s counsel and confidence; such an office of trust is honoured in Scripture. A true friend loves at all times, and the counsel of the faithful is a treasure to a king; Zabud’s place reminds us that those who bear rule need trusted and honest companions about them.

The title “the king’s friend” also lifts the heart to a greater friendship. The LORD called Abraham His friend, and the Lord Jesus calls His disciples friends, saying, “Henceforth I call you not servants… but I have called you friends” (Jn 15:15). Zabud’s honour near Solomon is a faint shadow of the friendship with God into which His people are brought through Christ, the greater than Solomon.
